source.title: An analytic theory of generalization dynamics and transfer learning in deep linear networks

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares learning dynamics for structured and randomized data in deep linear networks, a different setting and measure from the original image-label experiments.
record.gate_note: The study's own randomized-data comparison is in Figure 6. The text says randomized data is learned more slowly, but does not state an exact terminal training error or test error. Results cited from Zhang et al. (2016) and Arpit et al. (2017) are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study tests V6 through analytic and simulated learning dynamics: strong task modes are learned before noise modes, and structured targets produce earlier training-error drops than randomized targets. Its synthetic regression setting does not establish the classification and optimization claims in V1–V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate for the randomized-data comparison: randomization spreads signal variance across many modes and delays initial learning. The authors also conclude that networks learn strong task structure before noise, with qualitatively similar dynamics in nonlinear networks.
record.recipe_differences: Uses batch gradient descent in a teacher-student deep linear network with orthonormal inputs and randomized Gaussian outputs; does not reproduce the original image-label experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports slower alignment in deeper randomly initialized networks; Figure 6's randomized-data comparison does not vary network depth explicitly in its caption.
record.problems: The randomized-data result is presented as a figure and described qualitatively; the text gives no numerical learning-time comparison or explicit terminal training/test errors. The randomized-output setup is not an image classification experiment.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying results on the listed versions were reported. Other results concern generalization dynamics, transfer, or nonlinear networks on structured tasks.

untested.parts: Random classification labels, zero or near-zero classification training error, chance test error, and fitting with unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters under stochastic gradient methods.
The total time required to fit random versus true labels, the small constant-factor bound, and convergence across increasing fractions of corrupted labels.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs to zero training error. Appendix G's Gaussian inputs are used to study generalization, not this fitting claim.
A random-label corruption-fraction sweep with perfect training fit and test error rising toward chance.
Comparisons involving weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, or their removal.
Discrete classification labels and real datasets; the study uses synthetic teacher-generated continuous targets with additive noise or fully randomized Gaussian targets.

missing.what: Signal-before-noise dynamics within the same noisy training set: strong teacher modes are learned first, reducing training and test errors; later noise-mode learning further reduces training error while increasing test error. Record separate results for linear students and the qualitative nonlinear replication.

record.verdict_notes: Missing terminal errors or untested corruption fractions are evidence gaps, not grounds for limits_scope verdicts. The text explicitly establishes asymptotically zero regression training error for full-rank linear students in Section 3.3, but that does not establish V1's classification claim.

versions.untested_parts: Tests randomized outputs in a deep linear network; does not test image labels, standard nonlinear networks, chance test error, or unchanged original hyperparameters.
Compares structured and randomized data qualitatively; does not quantify a small constant factor in training time or vary the fraction of corrupted labels.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment.
No sweep over fractions of corrupted labels or corresponding training and test errors.
No weight-decay, dropout, or data-augmentation comparison.
The study compares structured data with fully randomized outputs; it does not test when real patterns versus noisy labels are learned within partially corrupted data.

rows.measure: Learning curves; the text reports randomized data is learned more slowly than structured data.
rows.note: The figure caption describes singular-value distributions and learning curves. The text states the qualitative slower-learning result but gives no numeric values or explicit terminal training/test errors.
rows.check: Figure 6 establishes different learning dynamics for structured and randomized continuous targets, bearing on V6. It does not report zero classification error, chance test error, time to fit within a small constant factor, or a corruption-fraction sweep. Replace the generic slower-learning value with slower initial training-error drops. The evidence is stated in Section 3.5 as well as illustrated in Figure 6.
